assessment.nobel_worthiness: A direct image of light bent around a black-hole horizon is exactly the kind of clue from nature I want: it turns decades of theory about the most extreme objects in gravity into a measurement, with the shadow size consistent with general relativity for M87* and Sgr A*. The conceptual and technical step (a planet-sized VLBI array at 1.3 mm) is original and its meaning for our picture of spacetime is easy to explain.
assessment.attribution: Doeleman led the mm-VLBI technical programme and the collaboration's push to horizon scales, while Falcke proposed the shadow imaging concept with Melia and was a driving scientific force. Zensus had an important institutional and VLBI role but I would favour Doeleman and Falcke as the two clearest decisive contributors. The collaboration is large, so any selection leaves out many; the allocation is not fully settled.
assessment.maturity: Results published 2019 and 2022, with polarization and multi-epoch follow-up, and independent reanalyses broadly agree. Interpretation of the shadow as a test of GR is robust at the level of the data, though precision tests are still limited.
uncertainties: Whether the committee regards imaging as a discovery or as instrumentation and technique.
Fair credit among the very large EHT collaboration and the concept originators (Melia is not in the supplied credit list).
Strength of GR tests from the shadow is limited by astrophysical modelling of the emission.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube opened neutrino astronomy by detecting a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos in 2013 and later associating neutrinos with TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane. This is a genuine new window on the Universe, a discovery driven by an instrument built to find something in nature, and with a clear link to the origin of cosmic rays.
assessment.attribution: Halzen conceived and led the project and Karle is the long-time senior experimental driver. The collaboration is very large, and others such as the original pioneers of neutrino telescopes (for instance the DUMAND and Baikal efforts) are not in the supplied credit, so a two-person configuration is defensible but leaves real attribution questions.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux is established at high significance and independently supported by analyses across channels. Source identification is still partial, with only a few sources at modest to evidence-level significance, so the field is mature enough for the discovery but not for its full astrophysical interpretation.
uncertainties: Source origin of most of the flux remains unresolved.
Credit to early neutrino-telescope pioneers and to the large collaboration is not captured by two names.
Whether the committee prefers to wait for KM3NeT or further confirmation of sources.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 invariant, followed by the HgTe experiment, opened the whole topological-materials field. It is a clean case of a prediction made precisely enough that experiment could confirm it, and it changed how we classify phases of matter.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele supplied the decisive theory (quantum spin Hall, Z2 classification). Molenkamp led the HgTe quantum-well experiment confirming edge transport, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal, whose authors are not in the supplied credit. That makes the configuration plausible but incomplete, since Zhang's role is a visible gap.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent experiments across materials and the field is well established, so recognition would be timely rather than premature. Topology has already been recognised in 2016 (Thouless, Haldane, Kosterlitz), which could argue for a longer wait.
uncertainties: Missing credit for the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal and for three-dimensional topological insulator work.
Overlap with the 2016 prize may weigh against it.
Technological payoff remains modest, though this matters less to me than the discovery itself.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea, gives timekeeping at the 10^-18 level and turns clocks into probes of gravitational redshift, fundamental constants and possible dark-matter couplings. It is a clean discovery-to-invention chain with direct links to fundamental physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and Ye drove the performance frontier with strontium clocks. This is a compact and fair pair, though the work relies on earlier frequency-comb and laser-cooling prizes and on parallel contributions by others (for example from NIST and PTB) not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Many independent labs have reproduced and surpassed the performance and international redefinition of the second is under discussion. The technology is well confirmed and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: The committee has recognised the frequency comb and ion-trap clocks already, so the incremental step may be judged smaller.
Possible competing credit to other clock groups.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Mott insulator transition and now allow controlled study of Hubbard-type models, with single-site imaging by quantum-gas microscopes. This lets one test many-body theory with real controllable systems, an experimental route that I regard as valuable because it gives clues from nature rather than only formal models.
assessment.attribution: Zoller (with Jaksch) proposed the Bose-Hubbard realisation, Greiner and Bloch carried out the Mott transition and later quantum-gas microscopy experiments. Greiner's role at Munich with Hänsch and Bloch is shared, and Jaksch is not in the supplied credit, so the allocation is plausible but not unique.
assessment.maturity: Extensively reproduced across many groups for two decades. Application to open questions in strongly correlated matter is still developing, so the discovery is mature while the payoff is partly still to come.
uncertainties: Credit among Greiner, Bloch, Hänsch and Jaksch, and Zoller's combined theory role.
Overlap with other cold-atom and quantum-information candidates on the longlist.
Whether simulation results have yet answered a question that was previously unreachable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Detecting and characterising atmospheres of planets around other stars through transit spectroscopy brings a question with real existential weight, the possibility of other worlds like ours, into measurable territory. The follow-on to the 2019 exoplanet discovery is natural, and JWST now reads molecules in these atmospheres.
assessment.attribution: Charbonneau made the first detection of an exoplanet atmosphere (sodium in HD 209458b) and Seager provided foundational theory for atmospheric characterisation. Tinetti has important mission and spectroscopic work but I judge the first two as the clearest decisive contributors. Other observers and theorists (for example Brown, Deming, Burrows) have competing claims.
assessment.maturity: Atmospheric detections are now routine with HST and JWST, but biosignature interpretation is still speculative and detections are contested in places, so the core discovery is mature while the most exciting implications are not.
uncertainties: Credit is spread across many observers and modellers.
Some reported molecule detections remain disputed.
Part of the field's appeal rests on future biosignature detection that has not happened.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing would be a new observational window on the cosmos, likely from supermassive black-hole binaries, and a test of gravity at wavelengths of light-years. That is exactly the type of finding that can reshape our view of black holes, which I care about.
assessment.attribution: Manchester and Kramer represent the long pulsar-timing programmes (PPTA, EPTA), Siemens is a leader of NANOGrav and its detection analysis. Several large collaborations (NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, CPTA, IPTA) reported independently, which makes any three or four names problematic, and Hellings-Downs earlier theory also matters.
assessment.maturity: The 2023 announcements showed evidence at about 2 to 4 sigma for the characteristic angular correlation, consistent across arrays but short of a definitive discovery. Recognition now would be premature relative to the usual standard of confirmation.
uncertainties: Significance is below discovery level and the source (black-hole binaries versus new physics) is not settled.
Credit across several independent collaborations is very hard to assign fairly.
Timing depends on IPTA combined data in the next few years.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Inflation, together with the quantum origin of density perturbations, explains flatness, horizon uniformity and the nearly scale-invariant spectrum seen in the CMB. Mukhanov's calculation of quantum fluctuations as seeds of structure is the part that connects directly to data. As a theorist I admire it, but I am wary of elegant theory not yet confirmed by decisive clues from nature.
assessment.attribution: Guth proposed the inflationary scenario, Linde the new and chaotic inflation that made it workable, and Mukhanov the quantum seed calculation. Starobinsky and Sato are major omissions and are not in the supplied credit, so the configuration is arguably incomplete and unfair. Priority questions among them are real.
assessment.maturity: Predictions of nearly scale-invariant Gaussian adiabatic fluctuations are well confirmed by Planck and other CMB data, but inflation itself lacks a smoking gun such as primordial gravitational waves, and alternatives and eternal-inflation conceptual problems persist. Recognition may be premature.
uncertainties: No detection of primordial B-modes, so the mechanism is not uniquely tested.
Omission of Starobinsky and Sato in the supplied credited names.
Concerns about the trans-Planckian and initial-condition problems, on which I have published, remain relevant.
